meta.title: Mission Designer: destinations, launch vehicles, subsystem rules of thumb, life cycle and presets
meta.note: Numbers marked 'estimate' are modelling assumptions for a Pre-Phase A concept study, not flight data. Launch-vehicle curves are rocket-equation estimates calibrated to one published payload each; the authoritative figures are on the NASA Launch Services Program (LSP) performance website.

destinations.name: The Moon
goals: Map water ice in permanently shadowed craters
destinations.payloadHint: A 12-unit CubeSat carries 2–5 kg of instruments; Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter carried about 100 kg.
destinations.note: No planetary launch window: the Moon comes round every 27.3 days, so this step shows the patched-conic transfer instead of a porkchop plot.

destinations.name: Mars
goals: Map buried ice and ancient shorelines from orbit
Relay data for rovers on the surface
Watch the atmosphere escape to space
destinations.payloadHint: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) carried about 139 kg of science instruments.

destinations.name: Venus
goals: Sample noble gases while descending through the atmosphere
Map the surface with radar from orbit
destinations.payloadHint: An entry probe with its heat shield weighs a few hundred kilograms; Venus Express carried about 93 kg of instruments.

destinations.name: Jupiter
goals: Search for a habitable ocean under Europa's ice
Map Jupiter's deep interior and magnetic field
destinations.payloadHint: Europa Clipper carries about 350 kg of instruments; Juno about 174 kg.

extraMass.label: Radiation vault
extraMass.how: titanium vault for the electronics (Juno's weighs about 200 kg)

destinations.note: Real Jupiter missions (Galileo, Juno, Europa Clipper) use gravity assists at Venus, Earth or Mars to cut the launch energy. Gravity assists are out of scope here: this tool designs the direct ballistic transfer.

destinations.name: Saturn
goals: Fly through the plumes of Enceladus
Measure the rings' mass and age
destinations.payloadHint: Cassini carried about 360 kg of instruments (plus the 350 kg Huygens probe).
destinations.note: Cassini reached Saturn with Venus-Venus-Earth-Jupiter gravity assists. Gravity assists are out of scope: this is the direct transfer.

destinations.name: Near-Earth asteroid (illustrative)
goals: Rendezvous, map and characterise a carbon-rich asteroid
destinations.payloadHint: OSIRIS-REx carried about 250 kg of instruments and sampling hardware.
destinations.note: ILLUSTRATIVE ORBIT: a Bennu-like shape and size (JPL Small-Body Database, rounded), but its position along the orbit is invented, so these launch windows are not those of any real asteroid.

vehicles.name: Starship

phases.label: Super Heavy booster (landing reserve held back)

check.label: 100–150 t to low Earth orbit, reusable: SpaceX's stated goal (the model expends the ship, so it predicts more)

vehicles.note: Speculative: no published beyond-orbit figure exists to calibrate against, so the loss term is fixed at 1.6 km/s, typical of the other vehicles here. Speculative: the vehicle is still in development. SpaceX's Mars plans rely on refilling in orbit, which is out of scope here.

spacecraft.fractionsSource: Typical planetary-spacecraft dry-mass fractions after SMAD Table 10-9 (rounded): power, telecommunications and propulsion are computed from their own equations instead.

power.notes: Array: triple-junction cells (~29 %) times packing, temperature and wiring losses gives η ≈ 0.21 at the start of life; 1.5 %/yr degradation; beyond 3 AU a low-intensity, low-temperature (LILT) penalty of 20 %; about 4 kg per m² with substrate and deployment. MMRTG: 110 W, 45 kg at launch, output falls ≈4 %/yr (NASA RPS). Bus electronics load ≈ 3.5 × (dry mass in kg)^0.6 W (estimate: about 220 W for a 1-tonne spacecraft). Battery sized for one hour of full load at 60 % depth of discharge, 120 Wh/kg.

link.notes: E_b/N_0 = 7 dB covers the channel code plus a link margin (as in the equation atlas). System losses: X-band 3 dB (circuit, pointing, polarisation, atmosphere), Ka-band 6 dB (adds about 3 dB for weather at 90 % availability). One 8-hour DSN pass per day. System noise temperatures typical of DSN 810-005.

isp.label: Cryogenic (liquid hydrogen / oxygen), 440 s — not yet flown on a planetary spacecraft

thermal.notes: Bus as a cube of 100 kg/m³ wrapped in multi-layer insulation (effective emittance 0.02, Gilmore). Heaters keep it above 0 °C (propellant lines must not freeze); 80 % of the bus electronics power counts as internal heat. Surfaces: sphere equilibrium temperature at the destination (cold case) and the closest point to the Sun (hot case).

spacecraft.maturitySource: Mass growth allowance falls as the design matures: about 30 % for a new concept, 20 % by PDR (AIAA S-120A-2015; JPL Design Principles D-17868).

lifecycle.name: Concept Studies
lifecycle.text: Find a mission worth flying and show that at least one concept closes: trajectory, launch vehicle, mass, power, data. This is a Team X study — and this page.

lifecycle.name: Concept & Technology Development
lifecycle.review: System Requirements Review (SRR), Mission / System Definition Review (MDR/SDR)
lifecycle.text: Write the requirements, pick the architecture, start maturing risky technology.

lifecycle.name: Preliminary Design & Technology Completion
lifecycle.text: A complete preliminary design with margins; the project is confirmed and its cost baselined (Key Decision Point C).

lifecycle.name: Final Design & Fabrication
lifecycle.review: Critical Design Review (CDR), System Integration Review (SIR)
lifecycle.text: Drawings are final; flight hardware and software are built.

lifecycle.name: Assembly, Integration & Test, Launch & Checkout
lifecycle.review: Operational Readiness Review (ORR), Flight Readiness Review (FRR)
lifecycle.text: Put it together, test it as it will fly, ship it, launch it, check it out in space.

lifecycle.name: Closeout
lifecycle.text: End the mission safely (planetary protection!) and archive the data.

c3.b: Characteristic energy (C3) is twice the orbital energy per kilogram the rocket must give you, C3 = v∞² in km²/s². Zero means just escaping Earth; Mars needs about 9, Jupiter about 80. The launch vehicle's payload falls steeply as C3 rises.

vinf.b: The speed a spacecraft still has when it has climbed out of a planet's gravity well. At departure it sets C3 = v∞²; at arrival it decides how hard you must brake to be captured — or how fast you hit the atmosphere.

porkchop.b: Every pixel is one solution of Lambert's problem: which orbit leaves Earth on this date and reaches the target after this many days? Colour is the launch energy. The cheap 'eye' repeats every synodic period, when the planets line up again. Type I transfers go less than halfway round the Sun, Type II more.
l: Hohmann transfer in the Orbit Lab

lambert.b: Given two positions and a flight time, find the connecting orbit. Here it is solved with universal variables (Curtis, Algorithm 5.2) and checked against Curtis Example 5.2 and the repository's Python toolkit.

hohmann.b: The idealised transfer between two circular, coplanar orbits: half an ellipse touching both. Real planets have eccentric, tilted orbits, so the best real transfer differs a little — the porkchop shows by how much.
l: Fly it in the Orbit Lab

dla.b: How far north or south of Earth's equator the departure v∞ points. From Cape Canaveral (28.5° N) a |DLA| above about 28.5° costs extra performance (a dog-leg or plane change). This model does not charge for it — a real study would.

lv.b: Each curve is the rocket equation run stage by stage, with one loss term fitted so the model hits a published payload (marked ◆). Treat them as estimates: the NASA Launch Services Program (LSP) performance website publishes the official curves that real proposals must use.

margin.b: Early designs always grow. NASA and JPL carry mass, power and data margins that shrink as the design matures, so that growth never breaks the mission. A design 'closes' when every margin is positive with room to spare.

mass.b: Payload, power, telecommunications and propulsion hardware are computed from their own equations; structure, thermal, attitude control, data handling and cabling are typical fractions of dry mass. Contingency is added on top, then propellant from the rocket equation.

power.b: Sunlight falls with the square of distance: an array that gives 1 kW at Earth gives 37 W at Jupiter and 11 W at Saturn. Juno and Europa Clipper still fly solar at Jupiter with huge arrays; beyond that, missions carry radioisotope generators, and plutonium-238 is scarce.

link.b: Friis's equation gives the power that reaches a Deep Space Network (DSN) dish; dividing by the energy each bit needs above the receiver's noise gives the data rate. Twice the distance means a quarter of the bits. Ka-band's shorter wavelength makes both dishes four times sharper each, but rain and pointing cost some of it back.

capture.b: Braking at the lowest point of the approach hyperbola is cheapest (the Oberth effect): Δv = √(v∞² + 2μ/r_p) − √(μ(2/r_p − 1/a)). A long, loose capture orbit costs far less than a low circular one; aerobraking can then lower it for free.

thermal.b: In vacuum a spacecraft only cools by radiating, so its temperature is set by the ratio of absorptivity to emissivity of its surfaces and the sunlight it receives. Blankets of multi-layer insulation (MLI) slow the heat leak; heaters make up the rest.

lighttime.b: Radio travels at the speed of light, so a command to Mars takes 3–22 minutes. Nothing at the destination can be flown by joystick: sequences are uploaded in advance and the spacecraft protects itself.

lifecycle.b: Every NASA flight project walks from Pre-Phase A to Phase F, passing Key Decision Points (KDPs) and technical reviews. This page is a Pre-Phase A concept study: its product is a concept that closes, presented at a Mission Concept Review (MCR).
